title: Interstitial Lung Disease: Recognize the Pattern and Refer Before Fibrosis Advances
bottomLine: Suspect ILD when progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, inspiratory crackles or restrictive/gas-transfer abnormalities do not fit common obstructive disease. Identify exposure, medication and connective-tissue causes, use HRCT/PFTs appropriately, and refer early because pattern classification determines prognosis and treatment.
recognize: Fine inspiratory crackles, clubbing, exertional desaturation and reduced diffusion capacity are important clues.
Autoimmune symptoms, occupational dust exposure, birds/mould, radiation and drugs such as amiodarone or selected cancer therapies can reveal the cause.
differentiate: Heart failure, COPD/asthma, infection and pulmonary vascular disease can mimic ILD symptoms.
A restrictive spirometry pattern does not prove ILD; total lung capacity and imaging are needed to define physiology/anatomy.
assessment: Take a detailed exposure, medication, autoimmune and smoking history; assess oxygenation at rest/exertion, crackles, clubbing and extrapulmonary connective-tissue findings.
workup: Use HRCT and full PFTs including DLCO when ILD is plausible; order autoimmune/exposure tests only when the phenotype supports them.
Before significant immunosuppression, follow current CTS infection-screening guidance.
management: Refer suspected fibrotic or progressive ILD to respirology/ILD expertise for multidisciplinary classification and disease-specific therapy.

Use oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination and comorbidity management according to need; acute hypoxemic deterioration requires urgent evaluation for infection, PE, pneumothorax or acute exacerbation.
medicationSafety: Do not start prolonged immunosuppression for an unclassified ILD before important infection and alternative diagnoses are considered.
Antifibrotic/immunomodulatory therapies have disease-specific indications and monitoring requirements.
redFlags: Possible connective-tissue or drug-induced organ-threatening disease
counselling: Explain why specialist pattern classification matters and review avoidance of a suspected harmful exposure when identified.
followUp: Track symptoms, oxygenation and lung-function trajectory; close the loop on specialty referral and exposure/autoimmune investigations.
examTrap: Calling low FVC 'restrictive lung disease' without confirming restriction or imaging—and starting steroids before excluding infection.
oneLinePearl: ILD care starts with pattern, cause and trajectory—not a generic steroid reflex.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current interstitial-lung-disease position statements and 2026 infection-screening guidance

title: Tuberculosis: Infection Screening Is Not Active-Disease Diagnosis
bottomLine: TB infection testing identifies immune sensitization; it does not distinguish latent infection from active disease. Before preventive treatment, exclude active TB clinically and with appropriate imaging/microbiology; suspected infectious pulmonary TB requires airborne precautions, public-health action and microbiologic confirmation/treatment without delay.
recognize: Prolonged cough, hemoptysis, fever/night sweats, weight loss or compatible imaging raise active pulmonary TB concern.
Risk increases with close exposure, birth/residence in higher-incidence settings, homelessness/congregate settings, immune suppression and some medical conditions.
differentiate: IGRA/TST positivity can support TB infection but cannot prove active TB.
A normal chest x-ray does not universally exclude extrapulmonary TB or very early disease in high-risk contexts.
assessment: Assess symptoms, exposure history, prior TB/testing/treatment, country/travel history, immune suppression, pregnancy and medication interactions.
workup: For suspected pulmonary TB, obtain appropriate respiratory specimens for molecular testing/smear/culture and chest imaging through the TB/public-health pathway.
Before latent-TB treatment, exclude active disease and check baseline tests/interactions appropriate to the regimen.
management: Use current Canadian TB Standards and jurisdictional TB programs for active and preventive treatment.
Isolate and notify public health promptly when infectious pulmonary TB is suspected according to local requirements.
medicationSafety: Rifamycins have major drug interactions; isoniazid/rifamycin regimens require hepatotoxicity assessment and regimen-specific monitoring.
Do not start latent-TB monotherapy in a patient whose symptoms/imaging could represent active disease.
redFlags: Possible infectious TB in a healthcare/congregate setting
counselling: Explain the difference between TB infection and disease, adherence importance, drug toxicity symptoms and public-health contact follow-up.
followUp: Ensure culture/susceptibility and public-health actions are closed-loop; document preventive-treatment completion when applicable.
examTrap: Treating a positive IGRA as latent TB without first checking for symptoms and active disease.
oneLinePearl: TB tests show infection history; active disease still needs a disease workup.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada TB resources

title: Lung Cancer Screening: Screen the Asymptomatic High-Risk Patient, Diagnose the Symptomatic One
bottomLine: Lung-cancer screening is an organized low-dose-CT pathway for asymptomatic people who meet current jurisdictional risk criteria. Hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, suspicious imaging or an already-followed pulmonary nodule requires diagnostic evaluation rather than routine screening intervals.
recognize: Smoking history and age/risk determine eligibility, but operational criteria differ across provincial programs and can change.
Screening benefit depends on willingness/fitness to pursue diagnostic evaluation and potentially curative treatment.
differentiate: Screening is not the same as surveillance of a known nodule or follow-up after treated cancer.
Chest x-ray is not a substitute for an organized low-dose-CT lung-cancer screening program.
assessment: Clarify symptoms first, then smoking exposure, prior lung cancer/nodule history, comorbidity, treatment candidacy and patient preference.
workup: Use the current provincial/territorial lung-screening pathway; symptomatic patients move to diagnostic chest imaging and referral pathways.
management: Refer eligible asymptomatic patients to the organized screening program where available.
Ensure abnormal screens receive diagnostic follow-up rather than simply repeating screening indefinitely.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric antibiotics for a suspicious lesion without an infectious syndrome solely to postpone definitive evaluation.
counselling: Discuss benefits, false positives, incidental findings and the need for follow-up; smoking cessation support should accompany screening without making abstinence a prerequisite for respectful care.
followUp: Track every abnormal screening result to diagnostic resolution and maintain the next screening date for eligible patients.
examTrap: Sending a patient with hemoptysis into a routine annual screening pathway instead of diagnostic evaluation.
sourceBasis: Ontario Health (Cancer Care Ontario) Ontario Lung Screening Program resources

title: Allergic Rhinitis and Sinusitis: Treat the Phenotype, Avoid Reflex Antibiotics
bottomLine: Allergic rhinitis is an inflammatory upper-airway disorder treated primarily with allergen reduction and intranasal therapy. Most acute rhinosinusitis is viral; reserve antibiotics for a bacterial pattern or complication rather than facial pressure or coloured mucus alone.
recognize: Allergic rhinitis often causes sneezing, itching, clear rhinorrhea and congestion with seasonal/perennial triggers.
Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis becomes more likely with persistent non-improving symptoms, severe onset or clear worsening after initial improvement.
differentiate: Purulent/coloured discharge alone does not prove bacterial sinusitis.
Unilateral severe pain, orbital findings, neurologic symptoms or recurrent focal disease requires a different workup.
assessment: Assess duration/pattern, allergy triggers, asthma, medication use, nasal obstruction/polyps, dental symptoms, immune status and pregnancy.
workup: Routine imaging is not needed for uncomplicated allergic rhinitis or typical acute sinusitis; use imaging/ENT assessment for complication, chronic/recurrent atypical disease or surgical questions.
management: Use intranasal corticosteroid and/or antihistamine strategies matched to symptoms for allergic rhinitis.
Use supportive care for viral rhinosinusitis and evidence-based antibiotics only when bacterial disease is likely.
medicationSafety: Topical decongestants used too long can cause rebound congestion.
Review sedating antihistamines/decongestants in older adults, hypertension and pregnancy.
counselling: Teach correct intranasal spray technique and why antibiotics do not shorten viral rhinosinusitis.
followUp: Reassess persistent/recurrent disease for chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy or structural pathology.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics because nasal mucus is green without considering duration, severity or double-worsening pattern.
oneLinePearl: Colour is not culture: sinusitis treatment follows the clinical pattern.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada antimicrobial stewardship principles

title: Acute Bronchitis vs Pneumonia: Decide Whether the Lung Parenchyma Is Involved
bottomLine: Acute bronchitis is usually viral and does not require antibiotics. Look for abnormal vital signs, focal lung findings, hypoxemia, frailty or other features that raise pneumonia probability and justify chest imaging or escalation.
recognize: Cough can persist for several weeks after uncomplicated acute bronchitis.
High fever, tachypnea, hypoxemia, focal crackles/egophony or systemic toxicity make pneumonia more likely.
differentiate: Coloured sputum does not reliably distinguish bacterial infection.
COPD/asthma exacerbation, heart failure, PE and pertussis can present with cough and need different management.
assessment: Check vital signs, oxygenation, focal chest findings, comorbidities, frailty, duration, pertussis exposure and respiratory distress.
workup: Chest x-ray is not routine for a low-risk patient with normal vitals/exam; obtain it when pneumonia probability is meaningfully elevated.
management: Use supportive care and safety-netting for uncomplicated bronchitis.
Treat radiographically/clinically supported pneumonia according to CAP guidance and severity.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine antibiotics for bronchitis and avoid opioid cough suppressants when risks exceed benefit.
counselling: Set expectations for cough duration and explain which worsening symptoms should prompt reassessment.
followUp: Reassess if symptoms worsen, new fever/dyspnea develops or cough persists beyond the expected recovery pattern.
examTrap: Giving antibiotics for green sputum despite normal vitals, normal oxygenation and no focal lung findings.
oneLinePearl: Bronchitis is a cough syndrome; pneumonia becomes likely when physiology or focal lung findings change.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Cold Standard and respiratory antimicrobial stewardship resources

title: Asthma: Confirm Variable Airflow Limitation and Use Anti-Inflammatory Treatment
bottomLine: Asthma is a variable respiratory syndrome that should be objectively confirmed when possible. Treatment includes inhaled corticosteroid-containing therapy, trigger/comorbidity management and an action plan; repeated short-acting bronchodilator use without anti-inflammatory control is unsafe chronic management.
recognize: Symptoms vary over time and include wheeze, cough, chest tightness and dyspnea, often triggered by exercise, allergens, viral illness or irritants.
Normal spirometry between episodes does not exclude asthma when variability has not yet been captured.
differentiate: COPD, vocal-cord dysfunction, heart failure, bronchiectasis and anxiety can mimic asthma.
Acute severity is determined by work of breathing, speech, oxygenation, airflow and response—not wheeze loudness.
assessment: Assess symptom frequency, nighttime waking, exacerbations/steroid use, SABA use, adherence, inhaler technique, smoking/vaping, occupational triggers and comorbid rhinitis/GERD/OSA.
workup: Use spirometry with bronchodilator testing and/or other objective variability testing according to age and clinical context.
Do not perform broad imaging/lab testing for typical stable asthma without another indication.
management: Use current CTS stepwise ICS-containing therapy matched to control and exacerbation risk; correct technique/adherence before unnecessary escalation.
Severe acute asthma requires urgent bronchodilator, systemic corticosteroid and oxygen/acute-care management according to severity.
medicationSafety: LABA should not be used without ICS in asthma.
Repeated systemic corticosteroid bursts carry cumulative metabolic, bone, infection and psychiatric harm.
counselling: Provide a written action plan, teach inhaler/spacer technique and explain controller versus reliever roles.
followUp: Reassess control, exacerbations, technique/adherence and lung function after changes; step down only after sustained control and risk review.
examTrap: Escalating medication without checking inhaler technique/adherence—or using LABA alone because symptoms seem intermittent.
oneLinePearl: Asthma management is objective diagnosis plus anti-inflammatory control, not rescue-bronchodilator dependence.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2021 Asthma Guideline Update
